lines.text: Rule of law.
A rechtsstaat is a country where the laws apply to everyone.
The authorities [overheid] must also obey the laws.
Everyone has the same rights, and a judge can make decisions independently [onafhankelijk].
Important values for many Dutch people:
Individual freedom [Individuele vrijheid]: every person may choose for themselves (party, faith, education, job).
This freedom became more important after the Second World War.
Emancipation [Emancipatie]: after 1960 women increasingly got the same opportunities as men — studying and working, not only being a housewife.
Minorities [Minderheden] such as LGBTIQ+ people [lhbtiq+'ers] have also gone through a period of emancipation and are still fighting for equal rights.
Tolerance [Tolerantie]: having no problem with people with a different culture or different customs.
Article 1 of the constitution.
The constitution [grondwet] is the most important law of the Netherlands.
Its first article states that everyone is equal and that discrimination is forbidden.
Men and women, all faiths and atheists, all skin colors, LGBTIQ+ people and people with a disability have the same rights.
Equal treatment.
You have the right to equal treatment [gelijke behandeling], for example in a job application [sollicitatie], a benefit claim or a school for your child.
Men and women have the same rights: the same chance of a job, the same salary [hetzelfde salaris] for the same job, boys and girls the same opportunity to study.
Yet there are still differences: women work parttime more often, men are more often a manager [leidinggevende], there is more violence against women, and women do more of the housework.
Freedom of expression.
You may give your own opinion [mening], and say and write what you want — including criticism of the government.
But you may not say what is forbidden by law: discrimination [discriminatie], for example, is forbidden.
If someone discriminates against you, you can go to court.
An opinion can also be hurtful [kwetsend].
Protesting [Protesteren] is allowed in the Netherlands; it is part of freedom of expression.
For example: signing a petition [petitie] (putting your name on a list) or holding a demonstration [demonstratie], usually in a big city like Den Haag or Amsterdam.
Freedom of religion.
Everyone may choose their own faith and have their own ideals.
You may gather with people of your faith.
The authorities may not decide what happens in a church or mosque.
Everyone must obey the law.
The law [wet] is more important than freedom of religion or freedom of expression.
A demonstration is not allowed on a highway.
You may not cover [bedekken] your face at school or on public transport [openbaar vervoer (OV)].
A church and a mosque must also obey the law: discrimination against the LGBTIQ+ group is forbidden there too.
The judge.
People go to the judge [rechter] when they disagree with each other; the judge decides what must happen.
The judge also imposes a punishment [straf] when someone breaks the law (punishable [strafbaar]).
A decision by the judge is called a ruling [uitspraak]; you must accept [accepteren] it.
If you disagree with it, you can go to a higher judge: to appeal [in hoger beroep gaan].
